name: Diet of Augsburg and the Augsburg Confession
teaser: Augsburg, 1530. Charles V held an imperial diet on the Turks and the split over religion. The Lutheran princes read him their confession; a Catholic reply followed, and the final decree ordered them back.
knownFor: The imperial diet at which seven Lutheran princes and two cities handed the Augsburg Confession to Charles V on 25 June 1530.
datesNote: 1530. Sarpi and Bensow say Charles summoned the Diet for 8 April. Bensow says the elector of Saxony reached Augsburg on 2 May. Pallavicino, Waterworth and Bensow have the emperor arrive on 15 June, the eve of Corpus Christi; Sarpi gives 13 June. Waterworth alone says the Diet opened on 20 June. The confession was read on 25 June, at three in the afternoon by Bensow's account. Waterworth and Bensow date the Catholic reply's reading to 3 August. Bensow dates the refusal of the Apology to 22 September. Bossert's heading and Waterworth date the final decree to 19 November, and Waterworth says it was published on 22 November.
issue: The emperor's summons, in the confession's preface. Charles called the Diet to deal with 'the Turk' and with 'dissensions in the matter of our holy religion and Christian Faith'. The views of the parties were to be 'heard in each other's presence'.
The four southern cities' preface, in Latin, says the same. It says Charles wanted to settle the grave and harmful split over religion that had troubled Germany for some years.

Bensow says that at Speyer in 1529 Charles had promised Clement VII to restore unity in the church. His first plan, Bensow says, was a general council, but the pope firmly opposed it. Needing help against the Turks, Bensow says, Charles invited the estates 'in very conciliatory words'.

What Charles meant to do. Waterworth, a Catholic historian, says he had resolved at Bologna to enforce the Edict of Worms. He would use all his efforts 'to reduce the Lutherans to the unity of the Church'. Sarpi says Charles left Bologna resolved that the separated princes 'should return to the obedience of the Church of Rome'.
Buchheim, a Protestant editor, quotes the writ's aim 'to settle the prevailing discord'. He holds that rooting out German 'heresy' was one of the emperor's main motives.

The pope's side. Sarpi, who wrote against the papal court, says Clement VII told his nuncio Vergerius to work 'that there should be no disputation in the Diet'. Nor, he says, was a council to be called in Germany.

The Lutheran case, in the confession. Their princes had appealed to 'a general, free Christian Council' and still held to that appeal. They asked only that the bishops 'allow the Gospel to be purely taught', and relax 'some few observances which cannot be kept without sin'.

The Reformed stood apart. Hinke, Zwingli's modern editor, says neither the Catholics nor the Lutherans 'would have anything to do with them'. He quotes Bucer to Zwingli on 23 June: 'Nothing more intolerant can be imagined than the hatred which the Lutherans have against us.'
calledBy: Charles V. The confession's preface says 'Your Imperial Majesty has summoned a Diet of the Empire here at Augsburg'. Sarpi says he called it from Bologna for 8 April, and Bensow gives the same day. No held source disputes it.
attended: No list of all those present is held, and no held source gives a total count. Pallavicino says the Diet met with an unusual attendance of princes, both church and lay. Sarpi says the reading hall held 'about 200', which is the size of the room.

Waterworth says the emperor came with the papal legate, Cardinal Campeggio, and 'a large retinue of princes, ambassadors, and electors'. Bensow says the elector of Saxony arrived on 2 May and waited over six weeks for him. The confession says its princes 'were among the first to be here'.

The confession's signers. Seven princes sign it. First come John, elector of Saxony, George of Brandenburg, Ernest of Lüneburg and Philip of Hesse. Then come John Frederick of Saxony, Francis of Lüneburg and Wolfgang of Anhalt. The senates of Nuremberg and Reutlingen sign after them. The list is the same in the English text, in Jacobs's Book of Concord and in Bensow's Swedish.

The final decree counts differently. It names 'the said Elector of Saxony, the five princes and six cities'. Bossert's note reads its first section, which lists the elector, George, Ernest, Francis, Philip and Wolfgang. The cities are Nuremberg, Reutlingen, Kempten, Heilbronn, Windsheim and Weissenburg. John Frederick is not in it, and no held text says when the four new cities joined.

The Saxon party. C. M. Jacobs, a modern editor, says the elector brought Luther, Melanchthon, Spalatin, Justus Jonas and Agricola. Bensow names Jonas, Agricola, Spalatin, Schnepf and Brenz as the Lutheran theologians at Augsburg, with the chancellor Brück.

The Catholic theologians. Waterworth names Faber, Eck and Cochlaeus as the most distinguished of those who wrote the reply. Bensow counts about twenty of them, and Hinke says Eck worked with seventy others.

The four cities. Waterworth says Bucer and Capito presented their confession to the emperor. Hinke says Jacob Sturm of Strasbourg sent Zwingli a copy of the Augsburg Confession on 31 May. Hinke also says Vadian was at Augsburg during the Diet and wrote to Zwingli.

The talks. Pallavicino names seven a side. For the Catholics he names Christoph, bishop of Augsburg, and a duke of Brunswick, later replaced by Duke George of Saxony. Two chancellors and the theologians Eck, Konrad Wimpina and a third, unclear in our copy, complete the side.
For the Lutherans, Pallavicino names John Frederick and George of Brandenburg, and the lawyers Gregor Brück and 'D. Heller'. The theologians were Melanchthon, Brenz and Schnepf.
decided: The reading, 25 June. Bensow says they met at three in the afternoon in the chapter hall of the bishop's palace, where the emperor lodged. The two Saxon chancellors, Brück and Beyer, stepped into the middle of the room. One held the German copy, the other the Latin.

Bensow says German was chosen after the elector of Saxony recalled that they stood on German soil. Beyer read it, and the reading took two hours. 'It is said', Bensow writes, that people in the palace courtyard understood every word.

Bensow says both copies had been signed before the reading. Afterwards Charles kept the Latin and gave the German to the elector of Mainz for the imperial archive. At the same time he forbade its publication.

Waterworth says the princes were then asked whether they dissented from the Catholic Church in anything more. They answered 'that the document presented contained all that they dissented from or complained of'. Pallavicino says the same.

A Catholic reply was ordered. Waterworth says the Catholic members resolved on it the day after the reading, with the legate and many theologians present. Bensow says the Catholic estates gave the task to Campeggio, who passed it to about twenty theologians.

The first draft went back. Waterworth says it was finished on 13 July and was 'required to be made shorter and less violent'. Bensow dates it to 12 July and says the emperor was angered at how Eck and his fellows had done the work.

The Catholic reply, called the Confutation by the Lutherans, was read on 3 August. Bensow says the imperial secretary Alexander Schweiss read it in the same hall as the confession. Waterworth says it was 'accepted by the Emperor as his own'.

Melanchthon, who was there, says the emperor 'demanded of our princes that they should assent to this confutation'. They asked for a copy, but 'could not obtain' one, 'unless on the most perilous conditions'.

Bensow gives the terms of 5 August. The princes could have a copy if they made no reply, showed it to no one and did not print it. Pallavicino gives the imperial side: their preachers had mocked the Edict of Worms, so no copy went out without that promise.
The princes would not assent. 'For in a matter pertaining to religion,' Melanchthon writes, 'how could they assent to a writing into which they had not looked?'

Talks were tried. Waterworth and Sarpi say seven a side met, then three. Sarpi says 'some few small points of Doctrine' were agreed, but 'no concord at all'. Pallavicino, answering Sarpi, says they agreed on the most important articles.

The Reformed confessions. Hinke says Zwingli's Account of the Faith reached the emperor on 8 July and the four cities' confession on 11 July. Sarpi says Charles had the cities' writing answered too, and refused them a copy.
Eck answered Zwingli in writing, dated 'Augsburg, July 17, 1530'. 'I have refuted Zwingli's pamphlet', he writes. Hinke judges that 'the emperor probably never read a line of it'.

The Apology was refused. Melanchthon says the princes offered it to the emperor, 'But His Imperial Majesty did not receive the offered writing.' Bensow says Brück handed it over on 22 September. It is told, he writes, that Charles was about to take it when Ferdinand whispered to him.

The final decree, 19 November, held in part. Its fourth section binds the elector, five princes and six cities to the emperor. They are to act 'against those who do not hold the most worthy sacrament, and the Anabaptists'. Its fortieth section keeps the law against the Anabaptists and orders children baptized with chrism.

The rest of the decree is not held, and its terms come from historians. Waterworth gives a draft of 22 September with a term to 15 April 1531. By then they were to say whether they would return, 'at least until the meeting of a General Council'.

Buchheim says the decree of 19 November carried the 15 April term. Waterworth says its final form proscribed the Zwinglians, ordered married priests degraded and destroyed monasteries rebuilt, and promised a council.
outcome: The Lutheran princes refused the decree. Waterworth says they opposed it, except for the clauses against the Anabaptists and Zwinglians, and refused their aid against the Turk. Melanchthon called it 'a horrible decree'.

Smalcald. Waterworth says the Protestant princes met there on 22 December and signed a treaty 'for their mutual defence'. His note says its form was drawn up on 31 December and signed on 4 January 1531. Buchheim says 'Even Luther was induced to approve of it.'

Rome. Sarpi says Clement VII was grieved that the emperor had received confessions and held talks. Most of all, Sarpi says, he was grieved by the promise of a council within six months. Waterworth says the 'events and proposals at Augsburgh' confirmed the emperor's hope in a general council.
The confession became a church's standard. Bensow says the Protestant estates endorsed the Apology at Schweinfurt in 1532. At Smalcald in 1537 all the theologians present signed it.
The 1580 preface to the Book of Concord roots its teaching in the confession offered 'at the Diet of Augsburg, in the year 1530'.

The Reformed parting. The Formula of Concord of 1577 says the 'Zwinglian teachers' separated from the Lutherans 'when this Confession was presented'. Pallavicino says the decree rejected the confession of the four Zwinglian cities.

Sweden. In 1593 the council at Uppsala bound the kingdom to the old, true and unaltered Augsburg Confession. It names the one handed to Emperor Charles the Fifth 'at the great diet in Augsburg' in 1530.
Denmark and Norway. Helweg prints the royal law of 1665. It binds the kings to the faith set out 'pure and unfalsified' in the Augsburg Confession of 1530.

The lost copies. Bensow says the two copies the emperor received have not been found, despite eager searches. He adds that Philip II may have destroyed them on purpose, and says only that it is possible.

traditions.name: Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations
traditions.note: Its princes and cities signed and read the confession (the confession's signers). They refused the Catholic reply and the decree (Melanchthon; Waterworth).

traditions.name: The Tridentine Church
traditions.note: The legate and Catholic theologians wrote the reply, and the emperor accepted it 'as his own' (Waterworth).

traditions.name: The Reformed Cities - Zurich & Geneva
traditions.note: Zwingli and four southern cities handed in their own confessions (Hinke). Waterworth says the decree proscribed the Zwinglians.

traditions.name: The Anabaptist Movements
traditions.note: The decree turned the estates against 'the Anabaptists' and kept the law against them (Bossert's extract). The confession also condemns them.

traditions.name: The Scandinavian Reformation Kingdoms
traditions.note: In 1593 Uppsala bound Sweden to the confession handed to Charles at Augsburg (Bensow prints the decree). Denmark-Norway's royal law of 1665 names it too (Helweg).

uncertain: Part of the Diet's own record is held: the signed confession, two sections of the final decree and the Reformed confessions. The Catholic reply is not among our sources. It reaches us through Melanchthon, who answered it, and through Catholic historians. Bensow, a Swedish Lutheran editor, gives the fullest day-by-day account.

Where the reading took place. Bensow says the chapter hall of the bishop's palace, where the emperor lodged. Waterworth says 'a chamber of the Palatinate palace', and Sarpi 'an Hall'. No held line says these are the same building.
The emperor's arrival. Pallavicino, Waterworth and Bensow say 15 June. Sarpi says 'the thirteenth of June', though he and Pallavicino both call it the eve of Corpus Christi.

Who wrote the Catholic reply, and how many. Waterworth names Faber, Eck and Cochlaeus, and Pallavicino names the same three. Bensow counts about twenty and makes Eck the harshest hand. Hinke says Eck worked 'with seventy other theologians'.
H. E. Jacobs calls Faber 'the chief composer of the Confutation'. Melanchthon names no one: 'certain theologians and monks'.
The first draft. Bensow dates it to 12 July and Waterworth to 13 July.
When the reply was ordered. Waterworth says the day after the reading; Bensow says a couple of days after.
Two counts of the Lutheran estates. The confession has seven princes and two cities. The decree has the elector, five princes and six cities. They are different documents of different dates.

How close the talks came. Sarpi says only a few small points were agreed. Pallavicino says the most important articles were. Buchheim blames the legate Campeggio for the failure. Each writes for a side.
The April term. Waterworth puts it in the draft read on 22 September. Buchheim puts it in the decree issued on 19 November.

Luther 'at' Augsburg. The Table Talk has him say 'At the Imperial Assembly at Augsburg, in the year 1530, the Bishop of Salzburg said unto me'. C. M. Jacobs and Bensow place him at Coburg for the whole Diet.
The Torgau meeting and Luther's journey. Bensow says Melanchthon came to Torgau on 27 March; C. M. Jacobs says 20 March. Bensow says Luther left Wittenberg on 3 April; C. M. Jacobs says 13 April.

Philip of Hesse's exit. Buchheim says he 'suddenly left Augsburg at the beginning of August'. Waterworth says he left 'under the plea of his wife's illness'. Foxe says he 'privily by night slipped out of the city'. No held source gives the day.
Eck's reply to Zwingli is dated 17 July in Eck's own text. Hinke elsewhere writes of 'Eck's answer of the 16th of August', perhaps the printed copy.
The day the talks began is unclear in our copy of Pallavicino; it may read 16 August. Buchheim says only 'August'.
Buchheim tells that George of Brandenburg offered his head rather than give up the word of God. No held witness of the time gives the story.
